1-start-here/1-welcome.html.description:
The full XRUIOS solution: one Manager, a worker per class, and a permission wall between every one of them.
This is the assembled system, ported from XRUIOS.Barebones onto the Plagues trust model. Barebones was one project with ~400 functions. Here each system class is its own worker process with its own password and its own key, and a single XRUIOS.Manager holds the master key, gates login, and brokers every request through a permission check.This wiki is about the permissions. If you want the function catalog, that lives in the Barebones wiki; here we cover the walls: the groups, the per-worker isolation, the login that unlocks everything, and how one program shares data with another without either of them touching a key they shouldn't.This is a project I knew I wanted to make back since 2017 and after thousands of hours of work, grinding and time it seems things are finally coming together.The XRUIOS.XR library and Linux Distro are next, although keep in mind the XRUIOS works on Linux and Windows right now. apps ──► XRUIOS.Manager (broker) ──► worker (one class) │ permission check │ its own key + password │ per-worker key handoff ▼ └────────────────────────► another worker One Manager per device. It takes a global lock on start; a second Manager steps aside. It holds the master key and never hands it out. A worker per class. 28 of them. Each compiles only its own class, so a breached worker doesn't even contain another class's code. Each gets its own password (PSK) and its own encryption key, both from the Manager. Nothing talks to a worker directly. Apps ask the Manager; the Manager checks the permission, then routes to the worker. Cross-class work goes worker → Manager → worker, so the same wall applies between workers. Process isolation. One class per worker. Compromise the Songs worker and you still can't reach Calendar's code - it isn't loaded there. Password isolation. Each worker has its own PSK. Only the Manager holds it, so only the Manager can talk to a worker, and a leaked PSK unlocks exactly one worker. Key isolation. Each worker's store is encrypted under its own key, derived from the master. A worker only ever receives its own key, so a breach reads its own data and nothing else. "Least privilege isn't a setting. It's the architecture."

1-start-here/1.1-what-is-the-xruios.html.title: 1.1 - What Is The XRUIOS
1-start-here/1.1-what-is-the-xruios.html.description:
This is the assembled XRUIOS system, ported from XRUIOS.Barebones onto the Plagues trust model. Barebones was originally one project containing roughly 400 functions. In XRUIOS, those responsibilities have been broken apart: each system class runs as its own worker process, with its own password, its own cryptographic key, and its own isolated permissions. A single XRUIOS.Manager holds the master key, controls authentication, and brokers requests through an explicit permission check.This wiki is about those permissions. If you want the function catalog, that lives in the Barebones wiki; here we cover the walls: the groups, the per-worker isolation, the authentication process that unlocks the system, and how one program can share data with another without either program ever receiving a key it should not possess.The XRUIOS is ultimately an attempt to build a spatial operating environment rather than simply another VR application.
There are already projects moving in this direction. Stardust XR, for example, approaches XR as a Linux display server and spatial environment where traditional 2D applications and native 3D applications can coexist in physical space. Other projects such as Ethereal Engine/XREngine approach the problem from the perspective of the open social spatial web, while WebXR-based systems demonstrate that immersive experiences can increasingly move between browsers, desktops, phones, and headsets.The XRUIOS takes inspiration from that general direction, but its priorities are somewhat different.The goal is not to make XR something that requires the user to understand OpenXR, runtimes, drivers, compositor architecture, IPC, certificates, permissions, or cryptographic identities before they can use it.The goal is to make those things disappear behind the operating environment.Install it. Run it. Open an application.Whether the user is wearing a headset, using AR glasses, sitting at a conventional monitor, or interacting with another device should be an implementation detail rather than a fundamental division in the platform.That means XRUIOS is designed around three principles:Spatial computing should not require spatial-computing expertise beyond making cool UIs and basic coding knowledge.An application should be able to request a capability from the operating environment without needing to understand the entire security architecture underneath it. The Manager, workers, authentication system, and permission model handle the complicated parts.The same philosophy applies to users. If a device can provide the capability, The XRUIOS should attempt to expose it through the same environment rather than forcing developers to create completely separate applications for every form factor.Security is not supposed to be something added after the system works.Every major system capability is isolated behind a worker boundary. Workers do not simply receive unrestricted access to the rest of XRUIOS; they receive the credentials and permissions necessary to perform their assigned role.The Manager is the trust anchor.Applications authenticate with the Manager, requests are evaluated against permissions, and the appropriate worker performs the operation. A compromised worker therefore should not automatically become a compromised operating system.This is the part where the XRUIOS differs significantly from the traditional "one giant application with a lot of internal classes" approach that Barebones started from.The walls are part of the architecture.The XRUIOS is intended to treat XR as one possible interface to a broader computing environment, rather than defining the entire operating system around a headset.A headset might provide spatial windows, hand tracking, eye tracking and a 3D environment.A desktop might provide conventional windows, keyboard and mouse.A phone or tablet might provide a touch interface.Another computer might provide compute, storage, sensors, or a specialized service.The underlying application and permission model should not have to be reinvented simply because the display or input device changed.This also means that the XRUIOS is not intended to be XR-only.If somebody has no headset whatsoever, they should still be able to use the same ecosystem through a conventional display. If somebody later buys an XR device, that device should become another interface into the same environment rather than requiring them to abandon the desktop version.That idea is visible in several modern XR projects already: WebXR applications can expose the same experience through ordinary browsers while providing an "Enter VR" path when compatible hardware is available, and projects such as Flock XR explicitly allow projects to remain usable in a normal browser even when VR functionality is enabled.Te XRUIOS is taking that concept further down into the operating-system architecture itself.A useful way to think about the landscape is: Stardust XR — a spatial display-server/environment approach for Linux, allowing 2D and 3D applications to coexist spatially. WebXR / immersive-web projects — make XR experiences accessible through browsers and allow the same content to potentially work across conventional screens and XR devices. Ethereal Engine / XREngine — approaches the problem as an open social/spatial platform, with worlds, avatars, applications, and communication. XR desktop projects — focus on bringing conventional desktop computing into spatial displays, such as head-tracked virtual monitors. The XRUIOS — combines the spatial-computing idea with a general-purpose, cross-device application environment and a strongly isolated permission architecture, with usability and security treated as first-class requirements. The XRUIOS isn't trying to win by saying "we invented spatial computing."It is trying to answer a more practical question: What would happen if a spatial operating environment were designed from the beginning to be easy to use, secure by default, and capable of existing on devices that aren't even XR devices? The answer is what this project is becoming.This is also not a project that appeared overnight.I knew I wanted to build something like XRUIOS as far back as 2017.What started as an idea for a spatial operating system eventually became years of experimentation: hardware, rendering, input, tracking, operating-system architecture, application APIs, IPC, authentication, permissions, and eventually the realization that the system needed actual security boundaries rather than simply a large collection of cooperating classes.After thousands of hours of work, countless rewrites, and more than a few architectural mistakes along the way, the pieces are finally beginning to converge.The XRUIOS is the result of that process.The objective is no longer simply to make a VR interface.It is to build a computing environment where XR is a first-class interface, security is built into the architecture, applications can communicate without sharing trust they shouldn't have, and the same ecosystem remains useful even when the user isn't wearing a headset.

1-start-here/3-todo.html.title: 3 - ToDo
1-start-here/3-todo.html.description:
NotaryGuard no longer trusts on first use. The Manager signs each worker's and app's file tree (XRUIOS.Manager baseline), and a worker only accepts a tree carrying that signature.
AllowAllPermissionGate removed from every worker. The default is ManagerOnlyGate. The old class is marked obsolete.
Hardcoded "Test" key and the ./XRUIOS fallback paths removed. An unbound context throws; XRUIOS_DEV_STANDALONE=1 gives a random per-machine dev key.
App registry. Every app gets a fresh password each run, held only in Manager memory. Standalone apps enroll over a pipe after the Manager checks the calling process and its folder. Third-party apps install from a manifest.
Audit trail. The Manager and every worker keep a chained HMAC log. XRUIOS.Manager audit checks every chain, and the Manager's own log anchors each worker log so a cut-off tail is noticed.
ServiceHost and AutostartInstaller. Windows Service, Windows logon task and Linux systemd user unit.
SecureStore folder permissions. The folder that holds worker addresses is now restricted to the current account when it is first used.
Staggered worker launch, so 28 workers do not start at once and exhaust memory.
Memory. Workers use workstation garbage collection instead of the Web SDK's server GC, the folder check hashes one file at a time (the old pass hashed 20 at once and grew every worker by about 100 MB), and the Alarm scheduler uses 2 threads instead of up to 20. All 28 workers together use between about 450 and 830 MB of private memory (16 to 29 MB each, depending on free memory) and it stays flat.
Permission rate limit. The permission store allows 100 checks a minute per app. The Manager now remembers answers for 15 seconds, and a store failure is reported plainly.
Every worker has real capabilities (140 in total). The last eleven were Timer, RecentlyRecorded, Processes, Note, AreaManager, DataManager, Creator, MediaTagger, Identity, Songs and MusicPlayer.
CertificateVault. Persistent, signed by the Manager's identity, with cert add / list / verify / remove and a check at start.
End-to-end tests in the repo (src/XRUIOS.E2E, run with run-e2e.ps1) on a throwaway data root.
.gitignore. Build output is no longer tracked. Implement WalkerWorks, the certificate issuance system. Until it exists, the Manager signs baselines itself. The vault holds certificates, but nothing else consumes a trusted certificate yet.
A version without WalkerWorks may be the better path. Not exposed on purpose or not yet: Identity does not create operating-system accounts or check OS passwords.
Note does not edit the notes inside a journal's categories.
AreaManager does not edit the objects inside a world point.
Songs does not read tags (title, artist) from audio files; MusicPlayer takes them from the player app. Linux login seal. Only Windows can unlock without a password at the moment. An installer. There is no installer yet.

1-start-here/4-where-it-stands.html.title: 4 - Where It Stands
1-start-here/4-where-it-stands.html.description: A plain account of where the XRUIOS is, and how far it has come since the wiki and the code were last in step (24 August, commit 3896f06). Where the memory went: the Web SDK turns on the server garbage collector, and the folder check hashed 20 files at once every 30 seconds in every worker. Together they grew each worker by roughly 100 MB. Now one file is hashed at a time (same hashes, so approved baselines stay valid), and the hash costs about 50 ms per pass. Start-up: with 28 workers launching 3 at a time, the Manager took about 60 seconds from start to all workers up on a desktop PC (59.6 s and 63.6 s in two runs). Approving every folder took 6 seconds warm and over 4 minutes once, cold. Tests: the full suite passed on the last run, 180 passed and 0 failed, on a throwaway data root. It covers every worker, permission denials, the 300-call burst, enrollment, events, tamper detection and the certificate vault. UI apps hold placeholder content (Calendar, Time, Clipboard) and swallow errors in about 10 places. They connect and make real calls (the Time app was run against a live Manager), but the screens are not finished. (WIP) No installer. Setup today is login, baseline, start. (WIP) Yuuko Protocol across devices (a theme change reaching the headset, the desktop and a phone together) is not designed yet. (WIP) Not exposed on purpose: creating OS accounts and checking OS passwords (Identity), and a known weakness left as it was: the Identity class builds some PowerShell commands by pasting names and passwords into a string. (WIP) Songs cannot yet read titles and artists from audio tags (the tag-capability table exists, unconnected); the music player takes them from the player app. (WIP) No versioning of the wire format or the encrypted stores, so the Manager and its workers must be built together, and an updated worker needs baseline again. (WIP Maybe) WalkerWorks does not exist; the Manager signs baselines itself. (WIP) Related: 3 - ToDo · 7 - Proven at Runtime · 16 - The Big Map

2-permissions/1-the-model.html.title: 1 - The Model
2-permissions/1-the-model.html.description:
XRUIOS splits into permission groups, and every group is made of per-class workers. The group is how you reason about access; the worker is where the isolation actually lives.That's 28 workers. Each is its own executable (XRUIOS.Worker.<Class>), launched and supervised by the Manager.A shared library would put every class's code in one process. The permission check only guards the network boundary - it does nothing about code already loaded in memory. So a breached worker holding one big library could call any function in it, granted or not.Instead, each worker compiles only its own class. The Songs worker literally does not contain Calendar's code. There is nothing to reach.Cross-class calls go through the broker, never in-process. When a worker needs another class it asks the Manager, which permission-checks and routes to that worker. Same wall between workers as between apps and workers - and it's what lets an Android or macOS worker slot in later without changing any caller.1. Process isolation - one class per worker. Compromise a worker and you get its class, full stop. The other 27 classes aren't in that process.2. Password isolation - one PSK per worker. The Manager mints a fresh 256-bit password for each worker and hands it over out-of-band at launch. Only the Manager holds it, so only the Manager can complete a worker's handshake. A leaked PSK unlocks exactly one worker. On top of that, the worker verifies the Manager's signature, so a compromised worker (which holds only the Manager's public key) can't impersonate it.3. Key isolation - one key per worker. Each worker's store is encrypted under a key derived from the master (HKDF(master, "xruios-worker:<name>")). The Manager can reproduce any worker's key, but each worker only ever receives its own. A breach reads that worker's data and nothing else - see 2 - Login and Keys.
An app connects to the Manager's broker with its own app password + stable id. The Manager gave it both, either when it launched the app or after checking which program was asking (see 8 - Building a XRUIOS App). It asks for a capability by name. The broker checks the app's grant in XRUIOS.Permission - the encrypted {app → {capability: level}} store. Not granted means denied, before the request goes anywhere. If allowed, the broker relays it to the worker over the Eclipse channel, adds the real caller's id to the call, and returns the result. The broker and the worker each write the call to their audit log. The app never learns which worker answered, never holds a worker key, and never touches the OS directly.The point of three separate walls is that breaching one doesn't cascade. Concretely:The walls are independent on purpose: code isolation survives a key leak, key isolation survives a PSK leak, and the login gate survives everything downstream being wrong, because nothing downstream has a key until a human authenticates.
Next: how login unlocks all of this - 2 - Login and Keys.

2-permissions/2-login-and-keys.html.title: 2 - Login and Keys
2-permissions/2-login-and-keys.html.description: Login is the gate. Nothing the Manager guards can be decrypted until a user authenticates, because the master key stays sealed until then. This is the most important security piece in XRUIOS, so it gets its own page. XRUIOS password ──Argon2id──► KEK ──AES-256-GCM unwrap──► master key │ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ HKDF per worker HKDF for the permission store "xruios-worker:Calendar" "xruios-permissions" The same master key also gives the Manager three more keys, each with its own label: xruios-manager-identity (protects the Manager's signing keypair), xruios-app-registry (protects the installed-app list) and xruios-manager-audit (the Manager's audit log). A worker's audit log uses a further derivation of that worker's own key, so the audit key is never the key that encrypts the worker's data. The master key is a random 32 bytes, minted once per user. It is wrapped (AES-256-GCM) under a key an Argon2id KDF derives from the user's XRUIOS password (64 MiB, 3 passes). Only the salt, the wrapped bytes, and the KDF parameters are stored - never the master key or the password. Each user has a world-readable login file (<Public>/Users/<uuid>.login.json): username, avatar path, and the password vector (salt + wrapped master key + Argon2 params). Anyone can read it, which is the point - a login screen lists the users on the device. Nobody can use it without the password, because the master key inside is wrapped.Warm (already logged in). While the OS session is alive, the master key is also sealed with the platform vault - DPAPI (CurrentUser) on Windows. The Manager unseals it with no password prompt. This is the "you're already logged into the OS, don't ask again" path. (Linux/macOS fall back to the password until libsecret/Keychain is wired.)Cold (typed password). No seal, or a fresh machine: you enter the XRUIOS password, Argon2 derives the KEK, and the master key is unwrapped from the public file. A wrong password fails the GCM tag, which is indistinguishable from a corrupt file, by design.Either way, XRUIOS.Manager login seals the key to the session; XRUIOS.Manager run unseals it and provisions the workers. No login means the Manager comes up locked - no keys, no workers, nothing decrypts.Once unlocked, the master key never leaves the Manager. Every worker key comes from it by HKDF with the worker's name as the label, and the Manager hands each worker only its own key at launch (out-of-band, the same channel as the worker password). So: The Manager can reproduce any worker's key on demand. A worker holds one key and can decrypt one store. A breach of the Media worker can't read the Time store - it never had the key. When XRUIOS creates an OS account for a user, the OS password is autogenerated and encrypted under the XRUIOS-derived key, so the system can authenticate that account later without a human retyping it. A recovery path re-wraps the master key so a forgotten XRUIOS password isn't the end of the account. (The Identity worker already carries the OS-auth half of this - LogonUser on Windows, PAM on Linux.)Next: what a granted app can actually call, and how two programs share events - 3 - Capabilities and Sharing.

2-permissions/4-installing.html.title: 4 - Installing
2-permissions/4-installing.html.description:
One Manager per device supervises the workers and holds the keys. You'll wrap this in a proper installer; here's what it drives.XRUIOS.Manager login # create / unlock the account; seals the key to this OS session XRUIOS.Manager baseline # approve the built workers and apps (signs their file trees) XRUIOS.Manager start # launch detached in the background XRUIOS.Manager status # RUNNING / stopped XRUIOS.Manager stop login first-time-creates the account (username + XRUIOS password) and writes the public login file. After that, login unlocks it and seals the key so start and run come up already unlocked. No login and the Manager runs locked: no workers.baseline is required. A worker or app folder that has no Manager-signed baseline is never launched or enrolled. Run it again after every rebuild or update, because any changed file will fail the check. XRUIOS.Manager baseline Calendar approves just one.The deploy folder has the ready scripts: deploy/windows/install-autostart.ps1, deploy/windows/install-service.ps1, and deploy/linux/xruios.service. Everything is under %LocalAppData%\XRUIOS\: Data (worker data and the worker audit logs), Public (login files), Baselines (signed file trees) and Users\<uuid> (the Manager's identity, the grant store, the installed-app list and the Manager's audit log). The full table is in 14 - The Chain. Workers: found next to the Manager, or point XRUIOS_WORKERS_ROOT at the deploy folder so the Manager can launch them. Apps use XRUIOS_APPS_ROOT the same way. The Manager starts workers 3 at a time. On a machine with plenty of memory, XRUIOS_LAUNCH_PARALLEL raises that. Lay down the Manager, the 28 worker exes, the apps and libs/ together (or set XRUIOS_WORKERS_ROOT and XRUIOS_APPS_ROOT). Prompt the user to create their XRUIOS account (login). Run baseline so the Manager signs what you just installed. Register autostart: a logon task for a normal desktop, or the service for an always-on machine. On next start the Manager unlocks, checks each folder against its signed baseline and launches each worker (each with its own key and password), and the broker is up.

2-permissions/5-permission-catalog.html.title: 5 - Permission Catalog
2-permissions/5-permission-catalog.html.description: Every capability that exists today, by group and worker, with its arguments and which built-in apps hold it. A grant is simply the capability's name, for example GetEvents. There is no Group.Worker: prefix in the code: the Manager finds the worker by looking for the first one that announces that name, so capability names must be unique across all workers.Events are granted the same way, with the prefix Events., for example Events.AlarmFired. Every UI app also holds Events.ThemeChanged.Every worker also answers <Worker>.Ping (for example Chrono.Ping), a health probe. Only the diagnostics harness is granted these.All 28 workers now have real capabilities: 140 in total. The ones in the tables below marked "none" are not held by any built-in app yet; an app gets them through its manifest (see Granting at the end). Do note, another layer exists as well (The XRUIOS.Barebones) within the project, which is responsible for essentially a CRUD style language for getting and acting on functions, bringing the total count of functions way about the 400+ line.Replies are plain text so any client can read them. List replies use ; between rows and | between fields, for example ListAlbums returns id|title|count;id|title|count. In any text that came from a user, a | or ; is shown as / or , so a row can never be split by what is inside it.Calls are limited by the permission store, not by the worker XRUIOS.Permission allows 100 permission checks per minute per app. The Manager remembers each (app, capability) answer for 15 seconds, so an app can call the same capability as fast as it likes. An app that uses very many different capabilities in a minute can still reach 100 distinct checks; it then gets a plain "could not be completed, try again shortly" message instead of a crash. Timers live in memory and do not survive a restart of the Timer worker. When one finishes the worker only announces TimerFinished.A song is named by a folder id plus a plain file name (never a path); a listing also gives the full path so a player can open it. The type Media belongs to MediaTagger, so Creator refuses it.A session is a piece of the user's reality made of world points; a data slot groups sessions. Ids are lists separated by ;.Editing the notes inside a journal's categories is not exposed yet.Creating an operating-system account and checking an OS password are deliberately not exposed: a granted app could create accounts or guess passwords against a real one.Grants are not written by hand in the Manager any more. They come from an app's manifest: a name, the executable that may enroll as it, its capabilities and its events. Built-in apps have theirs in AppCatalog.cs. A third-party app ships a JSON file:{ "name": "MyCalendarWidget", "exe": "C:\\Apps\\MyCalendarWidget\\MyCalendarWidget.exe", "capabilities": [ "GetEvents", "ListCalendars" ], "events": [ "AlarmFired" ] } XRUIOS.Manager install-app manifest.json At every Manager start, each app is granted exactly what its manifest lists. A capability that an earlier version granted and the new manifest no longer lists is revoked. Anything not granted is denied at the broker before it reaches a worker. See 3 - Capabilities and Sharing for a worked example, and 8 - Building a XRUIOS App for complete apps.

2-permissions/6-aether-engine-integratio.title: 6 - Aether Engine Integration
2-permissions/6-aether-engine-integratio.description:
XRUIOS.Permissions is not only the gate for XRUIOS apps. It is the same gate the HangarBay / Aether Engine mod sandbox uses to decide what an untrusted mod may touch. To the permission store a mod is just another requester id, so "grant Photos to this app" and "grant Calendar-read to this mod" are the same operation against the same authority. There is exactly one policy engine on the device, and mods live inside it.Mod security in Aether is two complementary systems, and XRUIOS.Permissions is only one of them. untrusted mod DLL │ ├── CasCore ──────────► ambient authority is UNCALLABLE │ (CasSandboxedLoader System.IO, System.Net, Process, reflection-invoke, │ + CasModPolicy) Godot camera/mic/screen - the IL cannot call them at all │ └── the doors that remain ──► host broker ──► XRUIOS.Permissions (policy) │ keyed on the mod's ModId ▼ host performs the action on the mod's behalf (the mod never receives the raw handle / stream / key) CasCore (CasSandboxedLoader + CasModPolicy) is the code-access wall. A mod is loaded under a deny-by-default IL policy, so the dangerous APIs aren't gated - they're gone. The mod can't call File.Delete and be told "no"; the call is uncallable at the IL level. XRUIOS.Permissions is the policy wall for the few brokered doors that remain. CasCore removes the illegal paths; XRUIOS.Permissions governs the legal-but-privileged ones (read the calendar, write to a shared folder, use the mic). You need both. A policy engine alone can't stop a mod that calls System.IO directly; CasCore alone can't express "may read the calendar, may not delete events." One removes whole classes of attack, the other makes fine-grained decisions on what's left.A mod can't reach user data, so it asks. The gate is ModRegistry.IsAllowed(mod, capability), which delegates to PariahPermissionBroker.IsAllowed(mod.ModId, capability, level). If it returns true, the host performs the action and hands back the result. The mod never receives the file handle, the sensor stream, or an encryption key - only the outcome. Same shape as an XRUIOS app going through the Manager broker: the caller holds a capability, never the authority.ModProfile.ModId is derived from the Notary-verified reverse-DNS PackageId (com.hollvania.calendarwidget), assigned by the host at enrollment. A mod can't claim to be another mod to inherit its grants, because it never gets to state its own id - exactly like an XRUIOS app gets a Manager-minted app: id instead of naming itself. Without this, "grant Photos to the trusted mod" would be meaningless. Enroll(packageId) registers a signed mod with a stable ModId. Its grants persist across sessions, anchored to a Notary signature. EnrollEphemeral(label) registers an unsigned mod with a fresh ModId each session, so any grants are session-scoped and evaporate on restart. Unsigned code cannot bank trust over time - you can let someone try a random .dll, but it starts from zero every run. CreateFileSystem(mod, grantableRoots) returns a SandboxFileSystem. The mod always owns its private directory; every other directory is a named SandboxRoot that only opens when XRUIOS.Permissions grants the matching capability (e.g. fs.write:<root>). "Can this mod write here?" is the same IsAllowed check as "can this mod read the calendar?" - one store, one verb, whether the resource is a folder or an OS service. Sensors work the same way: camera/mic/screen are never on a mod's allow-list and are reachable only through a brokered device service the host holds.A mod might ask "can I write here?" thousands of times a frame. PariahPermissionBroker wraps the encrypted PermissionHandler store with a memo TTL (ModRegistry(handler, context, privateRoot, TimeSpan? memoTtl)), so a verdict is cached briefly instead of decrypting the store on every call. A grant or revoke invalidates it. You get the security of an encrypted policy store without paying the crypto cost on the hot path.ModRegistry takes the host's Handler + AppPermissionContext - the same PermissionHandler.Handler the XRUIOS Manager uses, and the host's AppKey that never leaves it. There is one permission authority on the device, and mods are just more requesters in it. No second, weaker path for mods to slip through; the store and the audit are shared with everything else XRUIOS gates.XRUIOS.AetherModTest drives the real handler exactly as PariahPermissionBroker does under the hood: stand up a store, enroll two mods by package id, grant one a single capability, and ask the gate to rule.// grant the calendar widget exactly one capability; the sketchy mod gets none await handler.ChangePermission(SD(saveDir), SD(permClass), SD("Time.Calendar:GetEvents"), SD("com.hollvania.calendarwidget"), SD(masterKey), SDInt(1)); bool allowed = await handler.CheckPermission(SD(saveDir), SD(permClass), SD(capability), SD(modId), SD(masterKey), requiredLevel: 1); The calendar widget reads events but can't delete them; the data-slurp mod, granted nothing, is refused outright - the identical gate the Höllvania calendar app hit for DeleteEvent. Mods and apps converge on one XRUIOS.Permissions authority.
Next: writing an app or mod against it - 8 - Building a XRUIOS App.

2-permissions/7-proven-at-runtime.html.title: 7 - Proven at Runtime
2-permissions/7-proven-at-runtime.html.description:
The permission model isn't just designed - it's been run end to end and attacked. This page is the evidence, in two parts: the original runs from when the model was first built, and the runs after the hardening work (signed baselines, the audit trail, the app registry).XRUIOS.Manager login demo <pw> # Argon2id wraps the master key; DPAPI seals it to the OS session XRUIOS.Manager baseline # sign the file tree of every built worker and app XRUIOS.Manager run --dev-creds # unseals, launches the workers, broker up XRUIOS.Diagnostics # connects as an app and probes everything Login created the user, wrote the public login file and the DPAPI seal. run unsealed the master key with no password prompt. 28 of 28 workers launched, in batches of 3 (Launching 28 workers, 3 at a time...). Each announced its own loopback port, its own Kyber public key and its own capability list. The app completed the post-quantum handshake (Kyber + AES-256-GCM): SECURE. The diagnostics harness reported 33 passed, 0 warnings, 0 failed across 33 probes: the handshake, a ping for each of the 28 workers, a Calendar add-then-read round-trip, and the two refusal checks. DeleteEvent (not granted) was refused: XRUIOS.Permission denied 'DeleteEvent' for app:diagnostics. A throwaway test harness (not part of the repo) ran 36 further checks over Calendar, Chrono, Stopwatch, MediaAlbum, Assistant, enrollment, events and alarms. All 36 passed. The console examples on 8 - Building a XRUIOS App (Agenda, Lap timer, Alarm watcher) were run against the live Manager with the credentials of built-in apps. The add and read worked, the delete was refused, the stopwatch laps parsed as documented, and the alarm event arrived. The assistant provider example was compiled but not run, and the Aether example was not built.
Every wall in 1 - The Model fired for real: process isolation (28 separate exes), password isolation (a PSK per worker), key isolation (an HKDF key per worker), and the permission check on the privileged call.That last row happens for real whenever a worker is rebuilt. The Manager compares the folder against the tree it signed, sees the files changed, and refuses to launch it until XRUIOS.Manager baseline is run again. The anti-tamper works because it catches a legitimate change it was not told about.
Each worker and the Manager keep a chained log (see 9 - XRUIOS.SecureLayer). Two edits to a real worker log were tried, followed by XRUIOS.Manager audit:The second row is why the Manager records each worker log's newest entry in its own log every 5 minutes and at shutdown. A cut-off tail is only caught for entries recorded before the cut. The most recent entries, since the last anchor, are not covered until the next one.

3-building/6-the-diagnostics-harness.htm.title: 6 - The Diagnostics Harness
3-building/6-the-diagnostics-harness.htm.description:
XRUIOS.Diagnostics is the fleet self-test - the old Program.cs test suite reborn for the ported architecture. Instead of calling each class in-process, it connects to the Manager broker as a normal app and exercises the live workers through it. It's the fastest way to answer "is the whole thing actually up and behaving?" - and the regression net to run before and after touching anything.Three things, end to end: Every worker is up and individually routable - each of the 28 answers its own <Worker>.Ping health probe. A real capability round-trips - Calendar AddEvent returns an id, then GetEvents reads it back. The permission wall holds - an ungranted call (DeleteEvent) and an unknown capability are both refused. The exit code is the number of hard failures, so it drops straight into CI or a pre-work smoke check.It's a plain broker client, same shape as the CMD app:<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"> <PropertyGroup> <OutputType>Exe</OutputType> <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings> <RootNamespace>XRUIOS.Diagnostics</RootNamespace> <AssemblyName>XRUIOS.Diagnostics</AssemblyName> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <ProjectReference Include="..\XRUIOS.SecureLayer\XRUIOS.SecureLayer.csproj" /> </ItemGroup> <ItemGroup> <PackageReference Include="Spectre.Console" Version="0.49.1" /> </ItemGroup> <ItemGroup> <Reference Include="EclipseProject"><HintPath>..\..\libs\EclipseProject.dll</HintPath></Reference> </ItemGroup> </Project> Nothing special: XRUIOS.SecureLayer for the client, EclipseProject.dll for the transport, Spectre.Console for the results table.Each worker exposes a uniform health probe - <Short>.Ping (Calendar.Ping, Alarm.Ping, …) that echoes its own identity. Because the broker routes by capability name, a unique name per worker is what lets the harness confirm each one individually. The harness holds the list of workers, pings each, then runs the Calendar round-trip and the two security probes:// liveness: ping every worker by its own name foreach (var w in workers) { string echo = await mgr.InvokeAsync<string>(w + ".Ping", new() { ["input"] = "diag" }); bool ok = echo.Contains("XRUIOS.Worker." + w); // it answered, and it's the right one } // security: this must be REFUSED (the app isn't granted DeleteEvent) try { await mgr.InvokeAsync<string>("DeleteEvent", new() { ["uid"] = "x" }); /* FAIL if it goes through */ } catch { /* PASS - refused by XRUIOS.Permission */ } The Manager grants the diagnostics app every <Worker>.Ping plus Calendar's GetEvents + AddEvent (but not DeleteEvent, so the refusal is a real test). That grant is data-driven in AppCatalog.BuiltIns() from WorkerCatalog.AllShortNames, so a new worker is granted its ping the moment it's in the catalog.The harness also has its own list of workers to ping (the workers array at the top of its Program.cs). Add a new worker there too, or the grant exists but nothing calls it. This was missed for Assistant once, which left the harness at 27 pings for 28 workers.Like any app, it finds its credentials from the environment, a creds file, or enrollment under the name diagnostics. For enrollment its folder must have been approved with XRUIOS.Manager baseline.With an unlocked Manager and the fleet up:dotnet run --project src/XRUIOS.Diagnostics A run against all 28 workers:Transport Post-quantum handshake PASS SECURE Liveness Songs.Ping PASS up + routable ... (all 28 workers) ... Calendar AddEvent PASS uid 81e19ab7-... Calendar GetEvents PASS event read back Security DeleteEvent (not granted) PASS refused: XRUIOS.Permission denied... Security Unknown capability PASS refused: XRUIOS.Permission denied... --------- 33 passed 0 warn 0 failed · 33 probes ---------
An earlier version of this page showed one WARN, because GetEvents returned nothing right after a write. The cause was a time zone read as UTC when an event's time was converted to local time, and it is fixed. The harness still has a WARN status for a read that comes back empty, in case something like it returns. See 7 - Proven at Runtime.The harness only round-trips Calendar so far. As more workers' curated surfaces are used, add real probes for them here - a granted round-trip and, where relevant, a denied call to prove the wall. The harness grows into a full behavioural test of the fleet, one worker at a time, without ever reaching past the broker.
Back to 1 - Project Types.

4-understanding-the-wiring/1-yuuko-proto.title: 1 - Yuuko Protocol.XRUIOS.Interfaces
4-understanding-the-wiring/1-yuuko-proto.description:
This is a DLL containing what is essentially the core of the XRUIOS and Yuuko Protocol equally.I created this because I didn't want to have to handle "Which file does this correspond to on this device?" later. It also makes a few cross platform things easier to deal with.An app is simple and has 8 records: The overview has The name of the app as a Yuuko Protocol Reference
The minimum required Yuuko Version (for future Yuuko Protocol updates that add completely new features not able to be worked with older versions, we will try to not make many of these on the WI side)
The developer ID
The public key
The UUID
The name of the app itself
A description and
The Primary Platform it supports (Linux CMD/Windows Desktop/ Etc. Parameters are a value we feed into an event (AKA a function) A name
Parameter Type (string, byte array, etc.)
if it's required
The default value (Optional) and
A list of choices (Objects, optional) Events are just functions you can push, built up of A name
A description
An optional list of parameters (AKA the last thing we just hit) and
The command that can be interpreted 4.OS Specific Apps are powerful, allowing you to get the same app for a different OS! This is useful for doing stuff like installing Yuuko Protocol across all your devices. Each is built of
1. The name of the OS
2. The version of the OS
3. The link to download it and
4. The Panel info (Which we will get into next)Since this deals with auto downloads, we sign each App through Notary and check it here for tampering. To begin, we have "panels". Don't think of it in the same way you normally think of panels. Instead, look at it like a "grid" within reality. It can be 2D, 3D or more but at the end of the day it's taking up some level of space. A panel contains a Mode (2D Like Desktop or CMD, 3D Like VR or MR, CMD For Command Line)
View (Maximized, Minimized and Widget)
As an example, Call of Duty is 2D Maximized while a simple graphical interface to access it could be considered 2D Minimized and a rainmeter style UI could be considered a 2D widget. Preferred Platform Mapping simply is "What does this app like?". This is important to include because it's possible to for example render a 2D view as 3D but it doesn't mean it's meant to be ran as such. Ever tried to do something between two operating systems but the way the files are interpreted are different completely in part due to their location? Bindings try to fix this issue. We simply reference files and such by a UUID rather than their path and figure out their connection from there.There is much more nuance to this, but let's look at a few bases for this.
FileRecord is built up of a UUID generated and the file name.
Directory is exactly this but for paths. Meaning you can name a folder "Default OS Level Documents Folder" or something as abstract as "My Movie Collection"
Bindings handles figuring out the directory from a UUID alongside resolving it. This means if you save the UUID of the folder (You should do this), the XRUIOS will either automatically figure it out or take in user input.Media handles this exact same sentiment at the file level.

4-understanding-the-wiring/5-xruios.work.title: 5 - XRUIOS.Worker
4-understanding-the-wiring/5-xruios.work.description:
The XRUIOS workers are the isolated OS-level programs the XRUIOS.Manager talks to. Each one is its own executable (XRUIOS.Worker.<Class>), compiles only its own system class, and receives its own password and its own encryption key from the Manager. Everything below is what a worker actually does when SecureWorkerHost.Run starts it, in order. Refuses to run without the Manager. A worker only starts when the Manager launched it (XRUIOS_MANAGER_MANAGED=1). Started by hand it prints a message and exits with code 2. For debugging one worker alone, set XRUIOS_DEV_STANDALONE=1; it then makes a throwaway secret that nobody holds, so nothing can call it. Hardens the process. It blocks DLL injection and starts a debugger watchdog. If a debugger attaches later, the worker wipes its PSK and exits with code 66. Reads what the Manager handed it through environment variables. Checks its own folder against the Manager's signed baseline. NotaryGuard verifies the Manager's signature over the tree, then Blake3-hashes every file in the worker's folder and compares. A bad signature, or any modified, missing or added file, exits with code 44. The same check repeats every 30 seconds while the worker runs. The Manager sees the exit, re-checks the folder, and restarts the worker (at most 3 times). Makes its Kyber keys, builds its capability table, opens its audit log. WorkerOcean scans the worker's assembly for [SeaOfDirac] methods. Listens on a loopback port that the OS picks (or a Unix socket on Linux), then writes its address, capabilities, public key and process id to the SecureStore under WorkerAnnouncement.StoreKey(<name>). The Manager waits for an announcement whose process id matches the process it just launched. It only serves the Manager. The handshake needs the worker's PSK, and enrollment needs a valid Manager signature over the caller's id. A caller that somehow had the PSK but not the Manager's private key is refused at enrollment, and the worker's ManagerOnlyGate refuses calls on any session the Manager did not open. It exposes only its own capabilities. Anything else returns "Capability not found". It never decides who an app is. The Manager already checked the app's grant. It stamps the calling app's id into the call as __xruios.caller, and the worker reads it through WorkerCall.CallerAppId when it wants to record who asked. It records every call. Each call, success or failure, is one entry in the worker's audit log (see 9 - XRUIOS.SecureLayer for the log format). The log is tamper-evident, not secret: a worker can write it and the Manager can verify it, but anyone who edits a line breaks the chain. It publishes events. WorkerEvents.Publish(name, payload) adds to a small in-memory log that the Manager long-polls.
Earlier versions of this page listed behaviours the code does not have. For clarity: there is no Shamir secret splitting (each worker's key is an HKDF derivation of the master), no heartbeat from worker to Manager, no revocation list, and no OS container or sandbox around a worker. A worker is a normal process. Its protection is the three walls in 1 - The Model, not process confinement.Workers used to be started with AllowAllPermissionGate, with the explanation that the Manager checks permissions. That was true but weak: it relied on nobody reaching the worker. The default gate is now ManagerOnlyGate, which serves a call only on a session whose enrollment carried the Manager's signature. AllowAllPermissionGate still exists but is marked [Obsolete], and no worker uses it.Per-app permission decisions still happen at the Manager's broker, not in the worker. Reaching a worker now needs all of: The worker's ephemeral address (published only in the user's SecureStore). The worker's 256-bit PSK (in Manager memory and the worker's environment). The Manager's private signing key, to sign the enrollment. A worker folder that still matches the Manager-signed baseline.

4-understanding-the-wiring/7-xruios.core.title: 7 - XRUIOS.Core
4-understanding-the-wiring/7-xruios.core.description: The XRUIOS Barebones Context Shim is the runtime environment provider that connects XRUIOS workers to their execution context. It serves as the bridge between the Manager's orchestration and the worker's operational environment.While seemingly simple, this is the most important file, quite literally acting as what everything else builds on.To begin, the XRUIOS.Core is what manages giving each worker the data path, the public path and each worker it's own encryption key.The Manager is the sole authority for context provision:The Manager passes context to workers through environment variables. These variables are passed from the Manager process to the worker process at launch, never touching disk.┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Master Key │ │ (held by Manager in memory) │ │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ │ │ Calendar Key Alarm Key Processes Key │ │ (worker 1) (worker 2) (worker 3) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The old fallback paths (./XRUIOS, ./XRUIOSPublic) and the hardcoded "Test" key are gone. If nothing has been bound, reading DataPath, PublicDataPath or encryptionKey throws XRUIOS context is not bound.To debug one worker without the Manager, set XRUIOS_DEV_STANDALONE=1. BindFromEnvironment then calls BindForDevelopment, which makes a disposable store:The key is random per machine, never a known string. The data is not the user's real data. A worker started this way still cannot be called by anything (see 5 - XRUIOS.Worker).

4-understanding-the-wiring/8-xruios.mana.title: 8 - XRUIOS.Manager
4-understanding-the-wiring/8-xruios.mana.description:
If the XRUIOS.Core was the most important, the XRUIOS Manager is by far the most comprehensive part of the system. This page goes through every file in src/XRUIOS.Manager and says what it does. For how the files connect to each other and to the rest of the solution, see 14 - The Chain.The Manager is one program with a set of command line verbs:The entry point. It prints the banner and sends the verb to ManagerHost (or ServiceHost / AutostartInstaller).The orchestration behind every verb. RunAsync goes through these steps in order: Take the single-instance lock (SingletonGuard). A second Manager exits with code 66. Harden the process against injection and debuggers. Unlock: read the sealed session copy of the master key (LoginService). No seal means the Manager stays locked and starts nothing. Build the trusted core: the permission store, the Manager's signing identity, the audit log, the per-run app credentials, the broker, the event pump, and the enrollment pipe. Launch the workers, a few at a time. The default is 3 at once because starting all of them together (each a full .NET and web server process) used more memory than a 16 GB machine had. XRUIOS_LAUNCH_PARALLEL changes the batch size. Every 5 minutes, and once more at shutdown, record each worker's audit head in the Manager's own log. --dev-creds (or XRUIOS_DEV_CREDS=1) also writes plaintext <app>.creds files into the Public folder so apps started from an IDE can find their credentials. Without it, any left-over .creds files are deleted at start, because a readable password would let any local process act as that app.A global named mutex (Global\XRUIOS.Manager.Singleton). Only one Manager exists per device.ServiceHost runs the Manager as a Windows Service (on Linux it just runs normally). AutostartInstaller registers it: a scheduled task at logon (install), a Windows Service at boot (install-service, needs an elevated shell), or a systemd user unit on Linux.Creates users and unlocks them. A user's master key is 32 random bytes, wrapped with AES-256-GCM under a key from Argon2id over the XRUIOS password (64 MiB, 3 passes, 4 lanes). On Windows a second copy is sealed with DPAPI for the current user, so the Manager can start without a password prompt. On Linux there is no seal yet, so the password is needed each cold start.Holds the master key while unlocked and derives every other key from it with HKDF-SHA256. Each purpose has its own label, so one key never decrypts another's data:The Manager's long-lived Dilithium keypair. It is created once per user and stored encrypted (SealedFile) under IdentityKey(). Because it is reused, a baseline signed today still verifies tomorrow. Workers only ever receive the public half.A tiny encrypted file format: AES-256-GCM, laid out as nonce, tag, then ciphertext. Read returns null for a missing file and throws if the file was tampered with. The identity and the installed-app list use it.
An implementation of the context interface (data path, public path, key). Workers actually receive those three values as environment variables, which XRUIOS.Core binds (see 7 - XRUIOS.Core).The Manager's "is this folder the one I approved" check. ApproveAsync Blake3-hashes a folder, signs the tree with the Manager's identity (BaselineSeal), and stores the tree and signature under Baselines. IsCleanAsync re-hashes and compares. A folder with no signed baseline is not trusted on first sight; it stays down until someone runs baseline. Revoke forgets an approval (used by uninstall-app).WorkerCatalog is the list of workers, each with its permission group (28 of them). It also finds each worker's built executable, looking in XRUIOS_WORKERS_ROOT first and then in the repo's src/workers build folders. A WorkerDescriptor is a name and an executable path; its folder is the executable's folder, and that folder is what gets hashed.
Launches a worker only if NotaryVerifier says its folder is clean. It makes the worker's 256-bit PSK, starts the process with its environment (see 5 - XRUIOS.Worker), and waits up to 20 seconds for an announcement whose process id matches. If a worker exits, the supervisor re-checks the folder and restarts it, at most 3 times. StopAll ends them on shutdown.A place to keep certificates safely, written for the day WalkerWorks issues them. A certificate goes in, the Manager encrypts it, signs the encrypted copy with its post-quantum identity key, and checks both before trusting it. Until WalkerWorks exists you add certificates yourself. Where. Users/<id>/Certificates: incoming (drop a file here and the Manager seals it at the next start; KeeperOfTomes notices what is new), sealed (the encrypted .sealed copy and its .sig), and ledger. Keys. The files are encrypted under a key derived for the vault only (xruios-certificate-vault), and signed with the Manager's identity key. That identity is stored, so a certificate sealed today still verifies tomorrow. (An earlier version made a new signing key on every run, which meant nothing it sealed could ever be checked again.) Commands. cert add <file> seals and verifies one file (names use letters, digits, ., -, _; up to 1 MB; an existing name must be removed first). cert list and cert verify re-check every sealed certificate (signature valid and decrypts) and show OK or INVALID; verify exits with code 3 if any is invalid. cert remove <name> forgets one. At start. Before the broker opens, the Manager seals anything in incoming, re-checks everything sealed, and writes cert-import or cert-invalid to its audit log. A certificate that no longer verifies is reported, not silently dropped. What it does not do yet. Nothing else in the Manager consumes a trusted certificate. Baselines are still signed by the Manager itself (NotaryVerifier); the vault is where WalkerWorks-issued certificates will wait. The built-in apps: the console sample, the 13 UI apps and the diagnostics harness, each with exactly the capabilities and events it may use. It also finds each app's executable, and holds LegacyGrants (grants an old version made that must now be revoked, for example PocketPal's old Recent). AppManifest is what an app is allowed to be: a name (its id is app:<name>), the executable that may enroll as it, its capabilities, and its events. AppRegistry makes a fresh 256-bit password for every app on every Manager start. It lives only in Manager memory. The broker looks an app's password up by its id. InstalledAppStore is the encrypted list of third-party apps and what each was granted last time, so a capability removed from a manifest is really revoked. Install a third-party app with a manifest file:{ "name": "MyWeather", "exe": "C:\\Apps\\MyWeather\\MyWeather.exe", "capabilities": [ "Current" ], "events": [ "WeatherUpdated" ] } Run XRUIOS.Manager install-app manifest.json, then restart the Manager. Names may use letters, digits, ., - and _, and may not reuse a built-in name.Apps can be their own executables. An app asks the Manager for credentials over a local pipe (xruios-manager-control). The Manager does not trust what the app says about itself. For one request at a time, it: Checks the app name is registered. Finds the real calling process from the pipe, and reads that process's executable path. Checks the process runs from the app's registered path. Checks the app's install folder against its approved baseline (NotaryVerifier). Only then returns the app id, its password and the broker address. The pipe also accepts spawn <app>, which has the Manager start a registered app with its credentials in the environment (XRUIOS_APP_ID, XRUIOS_APP_PSK, XRUIOS_BROKER_ADDR). Every enroll and spawn decision is written to the audit log.A thin wrapper over the external XRUIOS.Permission library. It stores {app id -> {capability -> level}} in an encrypted file under the permission key. A grant is level 1, a revoke sets level 0, and a check requires level 1, so anything never granted is denied.Why it remembers answers. The store itself rate-limits every app to 100 checks per minute. Every call is a check, so an app calling faster than about once every 0.6 seconds (a slider drag, a window that polls) used to run out, and the failure came back as an opaque "Exception was thrown by handler". PermissionService now remembers each (app, capability) answer for 15 seconds, and a grant or revoke clears the memory. BrokerRouter also turns any remaining store failure into a plain message ("could not be completed, try again shortly") and a deny audit entry.The core that talks to applications. For each call it: Answers Events.Poll itself, filtered by the Events.<Name> grants of the app. Checks the app's grant. Denied calls are written to the audit log and refused. Finds the worker whose announced capabilities include the name (the first match). Removes any __xruios.* argument the app sent, adds the real caller as __xruios.caller, and relays the call to the worker over a pooled session. Re-encrypts the worker's exact result bytes onto the app's channel. A worker's error comes back as an ordinary failed response with the worker's own message, instead of an opaque handler error. The app never touches the worker, and the worker never sees the app.Keeps warm Eclipse sessions to each worker so the broker does not repeat the handshake (enroll, Kyber, Dilithium sign and verify) on every call. Because Eclipse numbers messages, one session carries one call at a time, so each worker gets a pool of up to 4. If the worker moved to a new address or a session expired, the pool reconnects and retries once. It does not retry when the worker itself reported a failure, so a call with a side effect is never run twice.WorkerEventPump keeps one long-polling session per worker (separate from the call pool, so a 20 second poll never blocks a real call) and copies each worker's events into EventHub. The hub is one ordered log of the last 2048 events with the Manager's own sequence numbers, so an app's cursor survives any worker restarting. Apps read it through Events.Poll.

4-understanding-the-wiring/9-xruios.secu.title: 9 - XRUIOS.SecureLayer
4-understanding-the-wiring/9-xruios.secu.description:
XRUIOS.SecureLayer is the library that the Manager, every worker, and every app share. It holds the encrypted channel, the capability dispatcher, the tamper checks and the audit log. Every file in it is listed here, grouped by job. For how these pieces connect to the Manager and workers, see 14 - The Chain.The client side of the Eclipse channel. One call to ConnectAsync does the whole enrollment, Kyber handshake and transcript check. After that, InvokeAsync<T>(capability, args) sends an encrypted call and decrypts the reply. Calls on one client are serialized (Eclipse numbers every message, so two calls cannot be in flight on one session). If the server says the session expired (idle), the client handshakes again and retries once. The server rejected the call before running anything, so that is safe. InvokeRawAsync returns the decrypted result bytes without deserializing. The Manager uses it to relay a worker's reply to an app without ever needing the reply's type. For a Manager-to-worker connection the caller passes the Manager's private key, and the client signs its own id with it. That signature travels in place of the client name. Hosts a worker (Run) or the Manager's broker (RunBrokerAsync) behind the Eclipse protocol. It contains PlaguesDiracService, which implements the five Eclipse calls: enroll, begin handshake, finish handshake, invoke, finish. On a worker, enrollment checks the Manager's signature over the client id, and only signed clients may handshake. A session the server no longer knows throws RpcException(Unauthenticated). That distinct status is what tells EclipseSecureClient it is safe to reconnect. RunBrokerAsync is the same host with a per-app PSK lookup and a router instead of a local dispatcher. HardenProcess blocks injection and watches for a debugger. The Manager calls it too. A single lock around the post-quantum crypto calls (Kyber and Dilithium). Pariah's primitives are not safe to call from several threads at once, which showed up as failed handshakes under parallel load. Only the crypto step is held, never a network round trip.
How an app that is its own executable gets credentials. EnrollAsync(appName) connects to the Manager's local control pipe (xruios-manager-control) and asks to be enrolled. The Manager checks which process is calling and which folder it runs from before answering. The answer is an AppProvisioning: the app id, its PSK (base64) and the broker address. Nothing is stored on disk. The pipe check is described in 8 - XRUIOS.Manager.What a worker tells the Manager at startup: its name, address, capability list, Kyber public key and process id. Only public information. The private key never leaves the worker.A small key/value store of JSON files under %TEMP%\SECURE_STORE<username>. It is not encrypted and holds no secrets. It carries each worker's address and announcement, and the Manager's broker address. The first time a process uses it, the folder is created and restricted to the current account: on Windows the inherited permissions are removed and only that account is allowed (for the folder and everything created in it), and on Linux the folder is mode 700 and files are mode 600. A folder left by an older build is tightened the same way. This keeps other accounts out. It does not stop a program running as the same account, which is why nothing secret is stored here.The worker-side capability table. It scans the worker's assembly for [SeaOfDirac] methods, then on each call: Asks the gate if the session is allowed (ManagerOnlyGate by default). Handles the reserved names (__xruios.events for the event pump, __xruios.audithead for audit anchoring). These are never announced, so the broker cannot route an app to them. Strips any argument starting with __xruios., except the caller stamp, and binds the rest by name. A parameter with a C# default value may be left out, so a capability can gain an optional argument without breaking older callers. Runs the method (async methods are awaited), writes an audit entry, and encrypts the result. IPermissionGate is the worker's second wall. ManagerOnlyGate is the default: it answers true only for a session whose enrollment carried a valid Manager signature (SecureWorkerHost.IsVerifiedManagerSession). CapabilityAllowListGate permits a fixed list. AllowAllPermissionGate is [Obsolete] and is only for throwaway tests.WorkerCall.CallerAppId gives a capability the id of the app that made the current call (for example app:XRUIOS.App.PocketPal). The Manager stamps it, so an app cannot lie about it.Only the PublicAccount struct (name, last check, OS folder). The old IPublicAcc service is gone.Signing and checking of a folder's file tree. Digest makes a canonical SHA-256 over the sorted (path, hash) pairs. SignAsync signs that digest with the Manager's Dilithium key. VerifyAsync checks it with the Manager's public key. Relativize rewrites paths relative to the folder before comparing. The same folder can be spelled differently by two processes (a long path against an 8.3 short name), and comparing absolute paths caused false tamper failures. TreeEnv and SignatureEnv are the two environment variables the Manager uses to hand a worker its baseline. The worker's tamper check. AdoptSignedBaselineAsync accepts a baseline only if the Manager's signature verifies; the verified tree is then held in memory. VerifyOrExitAsync hashes the folder and exits with code 44 on any difference, and StartPeriodic repeats it every 30 seconds. The old trust-on-first-use behaviour only remains for XRUIOS_DEV_STANDALONE=1 runs, which have no Manager to ask.An append-only log in which every line carries the previous line's MAC and its own HMAC-SHA256 over its fields. Editing, reordering or deleting a line breaks the chain from that point on. An entry holds: sequence number, time, actor, action, target, ok, detail, previous MAC, and its own MAC. ForWorker builds a worker's log from XRUIOS_DATA_PATH and its own key (<Data>/Audit/<name>.log). With no key (a dev standalone run) there is no log. The log key is KeyFrom(baseKey), an HKDF derivation, so the audit key differs from the key that encrypts the worker's data. Append opens the file under an exclusive write handle and reads the last entry from the end of the file each time, so more than one process can write the same log. If the file stays busy it gives up quietly rather than fail a call. Head returns the newest entry's sequence number and MAC. The Manager records these as "anchors" in its own log, which is how an audit run notices entries cut off the end of a worker log. Verify walks the chain and names the first bad line. The shared event types. XruiosEvent is one thing that happened (a sequence number, the source worker, a name, a text payload, a time). XruiosEventProtocol holds the shared names: Events.Poll (what an app calls), __xruios.events (what the Manager calls on a worker), and the rule that receiving an event needs the grant Events.<Name>. WorkerEvents is the worker's own bounded log (512 entries) with an epoch id, so a restarted worker makes the Manager read from the start of the new log instead of an old cursor.The app side of events. It keeps a second session open under the id <appId>#events and long-polls Events.Poll, so waiting for events never blocks the app's normal calls. It reconnects with backoff (1 to 15 seconds) and resumes from its cursor. A handler that throws does not stop the stream.

4-understanding-the-wiring/10-xruios.aet.title: 10 - XRUIOS.AetherModTest
4-understanding-the-wiring/10-xruios.aet.description:
The Aether Engine mod permission system is the bridge between Aether's mod sandbox and XRUIOS.Permissions. Instead of Aether creating a completely separate permission system, every mod is treated as a requester in the same permission store used by XRUIOS apps. Each mod:
Has a unique identity based on its reverse-DNS package ID, such as com.hollvania.calendarwidget. In the real sandbox, this identity is tied to the mod's Notary-verified package.
Uses that identity when asking XRUIOS.Permissions whether it is allowed to perform an operation.
Is granted only the specific capabilities it needs. For example, the calendar widget can be granted Time.Calendar:GetEvents without being given permission to modify or delete calendar events.
Is denied by default when no permission has been granted. A mod cannot simply request a capability and receive it.
Has every capability checked against its own identity. com.hollvania.calendarwidget and com.evil.dataslurp are treated as completely separate requesters even if they ask for the same capability.
Cannot turn a read permission into a write permission. Having Time.Calendar:GetEvents does not grant Time.Calendar:DeleteEvent.
Uses the same Handler and permission store that XRUIOS uses for its other permission decisions, giving Aether a shared security authority rather than creating another independent permission database.
Is checked before the sandbox allows the mod to reach a protected capability. The permission result becomes the gate between the mod and the underlying XRUIOS capability.
For example:com.hollvania.calendarwidget └── Time.Calendar:GetEvents → ALLOW └── Time.Calendar:DeleteEvent → DENY com.evil.dataslurp └── Time.Calendar:GetEvents → DENY └── Time.Calendar:DeleteEvent → DENY
Aether mods don't get access simply because they're running inside the engine. Their identity is given separately, and XRUIOS.Permissions decides what that identity is allowed to do. In short, each mod is treated like an app.The important distinction is that the mod's identity answers:
"Who is asking?"
while XRUIOS.Permissions answers:
"Is that requester allowed to do this?"
So the security model becomes:Mod ↓
Mod Identity ↓
XRUIOS.Permissions ↓
Capability Check ↓
ALLOW / DENY ↓
Aether CasSandbox ↓
Protected XRUIOS capability
This means Aether Engine doesn't need to reinvent permissions for every mod. XRUIOS already has the authority that decides what each requester can access, while the CasSandbox enforces that decision before the mod reaches the protected capability.

4-understanding-the-wiring/13-xruios.int.title: 13 - XRUIOS.Interpreter
4-understanding-the-wiring/13-xruios.int.description: A worker's capability says what the user asked for ("set the volume to 40", "show this notification"). The Interpreter is the layer that decides how that happens on this machine. Workers call the Interpreter; the Interpreter talks to Windows, Linux, or an Aether Engine game acting as the shell.It targets both net10.0 and net8.0, so the same library works inside the workers and inside a Godot project. The platform backend. One object implementing IPlatformInterpreter, picked from the operating system (Windows or Linux), or replaced as a whole with XruiosInterpreter.Use(backend). Per-area overrides. A host swaps one area and keeps the OS behaviour for the rest, with XruiosInterpreter.Use<T>(interpreter). For example, notifications can become an in-world panel while audio stays on the OS. XruiosInterpreter.Current is always the platform backend with every override applied, including ones registered later.Each area is an interface with a Windows and a Linux implementation:Windows code is under Windows/, Linux code under Linux/. Helper programs are started by Shell, which always passes an explicit argument list and never goes through a shell, so text that came from an app (a notification body, a layout id) cannot be read as a command.Some things have no built-in behaviour because the XRUIOS cannot know them. A developer registers an interpreter, and the system calls it:XruiosInterpreter.Use<IThemeInterpreter>(new MyThemeApplier()); When something changes, a worker publishes an event (a name and a JSON payload). The names are constants in XruiosEventNames: ThemeChanged, NotificationPosted, NotificationDismissed, VolumeChanged, ExperimentalAudioChanged, EqChanged, AlarmFired, AlarmsChanged, WorldEventAdded, WeatherUpdated, KeyboardLayoutChanged, ClipboardChanged, AppLaunched, PowerRequested (sent before the action), AssistantAsked, AssistantAnswered, plus the three shell events below. An app receives an event only if it was granted Events.<Name>.InterpreterEvents.Dispatch(name, payload) turns a received event into a call on the matching registered interpreter, so an app that handles ThemeChanged only needs to register an IThemeInterpreter:An event with no matching interpreter, or a custom event, is raised on InterpreterEvents.Unhandled.AetherShellInterpreter is used when a worker is started with XRUIOS_SHELL=aether. It wraps the OS backend, and keeps the non-visual areas (audio, power, clipboard, keyboard, system info) on the OS. The visual areas become events for the engine to draw:The engine receives those events through AetherShell (see 15 - XRUIOS.Aether and Apps.Shared).

4-understanding-the-wiring/14-the-chain..title: 14 - The Chain
4-understanding-the-wiring/14-the-chain..description:
This page follows the real connections between projects, files and processes. Every arrow was checked against the source. If you want to know what a single file does, use the page for its project; if you want to know what happens next, use this page. Projects and what references what: 1. Project graph
How the Manager starts: 2. Manager startup
How a worker starts: 3. Worker startup
What one app call goes through: 4. One call, hop by hop
How an app gets its credentials: 5. App enrollment
How events travel: 6. Events
How a folder becomes trusted: 7. Approval and baselines
How actions are recorded: 8. Audit
Where each key comes from: 9. Key tree
Where everything is stored: 10. What lives on disk An arrow means "references". Workers get the same references through src/workers/Directory.Build.props, so no worker .csproj lists them.Things that are easy to get wrong: SecureLayer references Interpreter, not the other way round. SecureWorkerHost switches to the Aether shell interpreter when XRUIOS_SHELL=aether, and WorkerEvents uses EventJson from the Interpreter. A worker is not a library consumer of the Manager. The two never reference each other; they only meet over the encrypted channel. XRUIOS.Aether does not reference SecureLayer. It compiles six of its files directly, because Godot needs net8.0. The external libraries are DLLs in libs/. SecureLayer uses PariahCybersecurity, EclipseProject, EclipseLCL, SecureStore, NotaryCore and NotaryShared. The Manager adds PermissionHandler (XRUIOS.Permission) and KeeperOfTomes, plus its own copies of the Eclipse, Pariah and Notary DLLs. Workers get EclipseProject, PariahCybersecurity, KeeperOfTomes and Secure Store from Directory.Build.props. Files involved, in order: Program.cs, ManagerHost.cs, SingletonGuard.cs, LoginService.cs, KeyAuthority.cs, PermissionService.cs, ManagerIdentity.cs, SealedFile.cs, NotaryVerifier.cs, AppCatalog.cs, AppRegistry.cs, BrokerRouter.cs, WorkerEventPump.cs, EventHub.cs, AppLauncher.cs, WorkerCatalog.cs, WorkerSupervisor.cs. In SecureLayer: SecureWorkerHost.cs, AuditTrail.cs.A worker's own Program.cs is short. It binds the context and its own data, then calls SecureWorkerHost.Run. The capability file next to it (Capabilities.cs) is what WorkerOcean scans.An app calls AppShell.Broker.InvokeAsync<string>("GetEvents", ...). This is everything that happens, with the file for each hop.Two walls are crossed in that path: the app-to-Manager channel (steps 3 to 4 and 15 to 16), and the Manager-to-worker channel (steps 9 to 10 and 13 to 14). Each channel has its own keys.How an app comes to hold an id, a password and a broker address.The Manager makes the password again on every start, so it never exists on disk (except in a .creds file when --dev-creds is used on purpose).Each hop keeps its own cursor. If a worker restarts, its new epoch id makes the Manager read from the start of the new log. If the Manager restarts, an app's old cursor is detected as "ahead", and the app is told some events may have been missed.Rebuilding a worker changes its files, so it will not start until it is approved again. baseline with no names approves everything found; baseline Calendar approves one.The first check catches an edited or reordered line. The second catches a log that was cut short, which the chain alone cannot see.Separate from this tree, the passwords (PSKs) are plain random bytes: one per worker and one per app, made by the Manager at start and kept in memory.
The whole thing in one picture: 16 - The Big Map.

4-understanding-the-wiring/15-xruios.aet.title: 15 - XRUIOS.Aether and Apps.Shared
4-understanding-the-wiring/15-xruios.aet.description:
Two libraries sit on the app side of the broker. XRUIOS.Apps.Shared is what the desktop apps use. XRUIOS.Aether is what a Godot or Aether Engine project uses. Both open the same encrypted connection to the Manager that 3 - A CMD App opens by hand; they only package it.A net10.0 library that every UI app under src/apps references. It references XRUIOS.SecureLayer and XRUIOS.Interfaces.The one connection an app opens to the Manager. WorkerBroker.ConnectAsync(appName) finds credentials in this order and uses the first that works: Environment: XRUIOS_APP_ID, XRUIOS_APP_PSK and XRUIOS_BROKER_ADDR. The Manager sets these when it starts the app. Dev creds file: %LocalAppData%\XRUIOS\Public\<appName>.creds. This exists only while the Manager runs with --dev-creds. Enrollment: ask the running Manager over its control pipe. The Manager checks the caller is the registered executable in its approved folder. The address, the password and the id are never written into the app. An app cannot choose where to connect or invent a password: a copy of the executable on another machine, or running from a different folder, gets nothing. InvokeAsync<T>(capability, args) makes a call, and Subscribe(onEvent) opens the event stream on its own session.A static holder. AppShell.InitializeAsync("XRUIOS.App.Time") connects once at page load, and from then on any page can use AppShell.Broker.A hole is a small static class under Holes/ that wraps one or two capabilities in a clean method, so a XAML page calls one line. For example TimeSource.ClockAsync() calls Now and parses the reply, and CalendarPicker.ListAsync() calls ListCalendars. The holes are: AppLaunchTarget, CalendarPicker, ClipboardHistory, EventFeed, KeyboardLayoutPicker, MediaAlbumPicker, NotificationFeed, PocketPalIntent, PowerControl, ThemePicker, TimeSource, VolumeMixer, WeatherFeed and WorldEventsFeed.A hole can only call what its app was granted. If a hole calls a capability that is missing from the app's entry in AppCatalog, the broker refuses it. When you add a hole, add its capabilities to the app's grant list in the same change.Live updates instead of polling. EventFeed.OnThemeChanged(handler) and the other On... methods return a stream; keep it as long as the page wants updates and dispose it afterwards. Callbacks arrive on a background thread.
Runs your assistant for the whole XRUIOS. Give it an IAssistantInterpreter and it answers every question asked through PocketPal. See the example in 8 - Building a XRUIOS App.WidgetChrome is the draggable borderless window content for the small apps (widgets). SceneCycler is a temporary development helper: an app registers named scenes, and a corner button cycles through them. It is meant to be deleted once an app has real navigation.A net8.0 library, because Godot .NET projects target net8.0 while the rest of the XRUIOS targets net10.0. Instead of referencing the net10 build, it compiles the client half of the secure layer from the same source files (EclipseSecureClient, PqcGate, XruiosEvents, XruiosEventStream, XruiosEnrollment, AppProvisioning) and references XRUIOS.Interpreter.The engine-side half of the Aether backend. The engine connects to the Manager as a normal app, receives the events it was granted, and hands each one to the interpreters it registered. ConnectAsync(appName, post, onError) finds credentials from the environment, or enrolls. The engine's executable must be registered with the Manager like any other app. InvokeAsync<T>(capability, args) calls any capability the engine was granted. Godot's scene tree can only be touched from the main thread, so every callback goes through post. In a Node, that is a => Callable.From(a).CallDeferred(). ShellNotify, ShellAppearance and ShellLaunch events go to the engine's INotificationInterpreter, IAppearanceInterpreter and IShellAppInterpreter. Events no registered interpreter handled are raised on the Unhandled event.
See 13 - XRUIOS.Interpreter for the interpreters and 8 - Building a XRUIOS App for a full example.
