4-understanding-the-wiring/16-the-big-ma.title: 16 - The Big Map
4-understanding-the-wiring/16-the-big-ma.description:
Every file that matters, in one picture, and how they talk to each other. Read it top to bottom: an app at the top asks for something, and the request travels down through the Manager to a worker and its data.How to read the arrows: A plain arrow is one file calling another. A thick arrow is an encrypted connection between two programs (post-quantum key exchange, then AES-256-GCM). A dotted arrow is reading or writing something on disk. A box with <br/> text is a file; the second line says what it does. The smaller pictures that show one story at a time (startup, one call, enrollment, events, approval, audit, keys) are on 14 - The Chain. This page is the whole thing at once. Apps never touch workers. An app page calls a hole, the hole calls WorkerBroker, and EclipseSecureClient carries the call over an encrypted connection to the Manager's broker. The app and the worker only ever meet inside the Manager. The Manager decides. BrokerRouter asks PermissionService (which remembers answers for 15 seconds because the permission library rate-limits to 100 checks a minute), picks the worker that announced the capability, relays it through a warm session, and writes both ends to the audit log. Workers are launched, not trusted. WorkerSupervisor only starts a worker whose folder matches a baseline the Manager signed, hands it a password, its own key and the signed baseline, and the worker checks itself again every 30 seconds. Every key comes from one password. LoginService unlocks the master key; KeyAuthority derives a separate key for each purpose (permissions, identity, app list, certificates, audit, and one per worker), so no store opens with another's key. The Interpreter is the only code that touches the machine. Capabilities ask it to change the volume, show a notification or open an app; on Windows and Linux it calls the OS, and under an Aether Engine shell it sends events for the engine to draw.
Every folder and file, plus the Yuuko Protocol repo: 17 - Every File and How They Connect.

4-understanding-the-wiring/17-every-file.title: 17 - Every File and How They Connect
4-understanding-the-wiring/17-every-file.description:
This page walks the whole tree, folder by folder, then the Yuuko Protocol repo, then shows where the two meet. Read 16 - The Big Map first for the picture; this page is the legend that goes with it.(I KNOW i'm gonna forget how the XRUIOS works and I hate myself for it, so this is what this is for)Two repos are covered: The XRUIOS (GitHub/The XRUIOS): the trusted core, 28 workers, the apps, the tests. Yuuko Protocol (GitHub/YuukoProtocol): pub/sub messaging, encrypted peer sessions, and the Bindings that make file locations portable between devices. An app asks the Manager for something. The Manager checks the app's permission, finds the worker that announced that capability, and relays the call over an encrypted channel. The worker runs the real logic in a class from src/systems, stores its data encrypted, and answers. Workers are only started if their folder matches a signature the Manager made. Yuuko Protocol is a separate library for talking between devices; today it shares code and the Eclipse crypto library with the XRUIOS, but no XRUIOS process calls it yet. XRUIOS.Contracts: IXruiosContext.cs (the paths and key a worker is handed) and PermissionGroup.cs (the 7 permission groups). XRUIOS.Core: XRUIOS.cs, the static holder each worker binds at start (data path, public path, its own key). An unbound context throws. src/systems/ (*Class.cs, Songs.cs, Processes.cs and so on): the real work, one file per system class: Alarm, Calendar, Clipboard, Identity, Note, Songs, Theme, Timer, Volume and the rest. Each has a CRUD set plus an initializer and stores its data encrypted under Data/<Class>.
XRUIOS.Systems: a project of its own beside the logic folder (see 3 - XRUIOS.Systems for what the classes do). XRUIOS.Interfaces/Functions/: the records and types those classes use, such as SongOverview. Apps may reference these without referencing any logic. Songs.cs also holds the audio tag capability table, unused for now. XruiosInterpreter.cs picks a backend. Windows/* and Linux/* call the operating system (audio, power, clipboard...). AetherShellInterpreter.cs instead sends events for a game engine to draw. DeveloperInterpreters.cs holds event names and Dispatch. XRUIOS.Interpreter.Probe is a small program that exercises it.28 folders, one per system class: Alarm, App, AreaManager, Assistant, Calendar, Chrono, Clipboard, Creator, DataManager, DeviceManager, ExperimentalVolume, Geo, Identity, MediaAlbum, MediaTagger, MusicPlayer, Note, Notification, Processes, RecentlyRecorded, Songs, SoundEQ, Stopwatch, SystemInfo, Theme, Timer, Volume, WorldEvents. Each has the same two files: Program.cs: bind the context, initialize the class, hand control to SecureWorkerHost. Capabilities.cs: the [SeaOfDirac] methods, the only way in. To add a capability you edit only this file. src/workers/Directory.Build.props gives every worker workstation garbage collection, which keeps each worker between about 16 and 29 MB. XRUIOS.Apps.Shared: what apps build on. WorkerBroker.cs finds credentials, AppShell.cs connects once, Holes/*.cs are one-line wrappers per capability, Holes/EventFeed.cs delivers live updates, AssistantProvider.cs plugs in your own AI. XRUIOS.App.*: 13 apps (AppLauncher, Calendar, Clipboard, Gallery, Keyboard, Notifications, PocketPal, Power, ThemeEditor, Time, VolumeManager, Weather, WorldEvents). XRUIOS.SampleApp: the smallest app that talks to the Manager. XRUIOS.Diagnostics: asks every worker a health question (33 probes). XRUIOS.Aether: AetherShell.cs, the library a game engine uses to act as a XRUIOS shell. XRUIOS.AetherModTest: shows an engine mod being treated as an app for permissions. Program.cs holds 20 sections (regression, burst, clock, calendars, albums, enrollment, assistant, events, alarm, timer, recent, processes, notes, areas, datamanager, creators, mediatags, identity, songs, musicplayer). run-e2e.ps1 builds a throwaway data root, creates an account, approves everything, starts the Manager, runs the sections and the diagnostics harness, then prints a memory table. e2e.harness.manifest.json grants the test app every capability. Last result: 180 passed, 0 failed.Layout: YuukoProtocol/YuukoProtocol/ is the library, YuukoProtocol/YuukoSandbox/ is a test and benchmark program, docs/ is the exported wiki, ZenohNative.targets fetches the native Zenoh library.How a request travels: the requester handshakes with the provider over topic yuuko/handshake, both derive the same lane keys, then the request goes over yuuko/eclipse/data encrypted on one lane, and the answer comes back on the same lane. The transport underneath (LocalBroker or Zenoh) only ever sees ciphertext after the handshake.MainTest.cs is an interactive demo (it waits for a key). Benchmark.cs (dotnet run --project YuukoSandbox -- bench) measures handshake and request speed. YuukoTopics.cs holds the canonical topic names (yuuko/xruios/config, yuuko/xruios/events, yuuko/xruios/sync and others). Shared code, copied. src/YuukoProtocol.XRUIOS.Interfaces holds the same Backend files as the Yuuko repo (identical now, except that the Yuuko repo's App.cs has one extra empty method, CreateSign). System classes that store media folders, such as Songs and MediaTagger, use it. Shared crypto. Both sides use the Eclipse DLLs and Pariah, but with separate sessions: the XRUIOS channel is Manager-to-worker on one device; Yuuko's is device-to-device. No live link. No XRUIOS process publishes to or subscribes on a Yuuko topic. A Yuuko app that does so would be installed like any other XRUIOS app (manifest, per-run password, granted capabilities), read local events, publish them on yuuko/xruios/events, and apply incoming packets by calling XRUIOS capabilities.
